Respiratory protective devices described in Table 1-1 must be approved under the provisions of 30 CFR 11. 9. Respirators specified for use in higher concentrations of 1,1,1-trichloroethane may also be used in atmospheres with lower concentrations. 10. 11. Chemical cartridges and canisters must not be used for durations exceeding those indicated in Table 1-1. 12. Chemical cartridges and canisters should be replaced after each day of use. 13. 14. Protective clothing must be worn in any operation where workers may come into direct contact with liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane. 15. The protective clothing should be resistant to 1,1,1-trichloroethane. 16. Gloves, boots, overshoes, and bib-type aprons that cover boot tops must be provided when necessary. 17. Impervious supplied-air hoods or suits must be worn when entering confined spaces such as pits or tanks unless it is known to be safe. 18. In situations where heat stress is likely to occur, air-supplied suits must be used. 19. All protective clothing must be well-aired and inspected for defects prior to reuse. 20. Hands that come into contact with liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane must be protected by impervious gloves. 21. Any liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane that contacts the skin should be promptly removed. 22. Containers delivered by closed truck or rail must not be unloaded until the vehicle has been ventilated. 23. The absence of any odor of 1,1,1-trichloroethane should not be used as a criterion for adequate ventilation. 24. Storage containers, piping, and valves must be periodically inspected for leakage. 25. Storage facilities must be designed to contain spills and prevent contamination of workroom air. 26. Processes and storage facilities must not be located near open flames or high-temperature operations unless precautions are taken to prevent fire and explosion hazards. 27. 28. Ventilation systems, if used, must be designed to prevent the accumulation or recirculation of 1,1,1-trichloroethane in the workroom and to effectively remove it from workers' breathing zones. 29. Adequate, uncontaminated make-up air must be provided. 30. 31. Portable exhaust ventilation or suitable general ventilation must be provided, if necessary, to limit environmental concentrations during nonroutine operations requiring the application of 1,1,1-trichloroethane. 32. Personnel entering confined spaces must be equipped with appropriate personal protective equipment and protected by a lifeline tended by another worker outside the space, who must also be equipped for entry with approved respiratory, eye, and skin protection, lifeline, and have contact with a third party. 33. 34. These instructions and procedures must be printed in both English and the predominant language of non-English-speaking workers, if any. 35. Special instructions must be given to illiterate workers. 36. Showers and eye wash facilities must be provided and readily accessible to workers in all areas where skin or eye splash with 1,1,1-trichloroethane is likely. 37. If 1,1,1-trichloroethane is splashed on a worker, contaminated clothing must be promptly removed, and the skin washed with soap and water. 38. If liquid 1,1,1-trichloroethane contacts the eyes, they must be thoroughly irrigated with clean water, promptly followed by medical assistance. 39. Such incidents must be reported to the immediate supervisor by the affected employee or by a fellow worker. 40. 41. If confirmed, control procedures must be instituted as soon as possible; these may precede and obviate confirmatory monitoring if the employer desires. 42. 43. 44. Normal monitoring may then be resumed. 45. 46. The number of TWA and ceiling concentration determinations for an operation must be based on factors such as the variations in location and job functions of workers in that operation. 47. Environmental monitoring records must be maintained for at least 20 years. 48. These records must include methods of sampling and analysis used, types of respiratory protection used, and TWA and ceiling concentrations found. 49. 50. 51. 52. These medical records must be made available to the designated medical representatives of the Secretary of Labor, the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, the employer, and the employee or former employee. 53. Further research is needed to more completely characterize the effects of certain levels of 1,1,1-trichloroethane on workers, especially epidemiological, chronic, and teratological studies. 54. Animal studies are underway at the National Cancer Institute to determine if 1,1,1-trichloroethane is carcinogenic. 55. Similar studies are being performed by the Dow Chemical Company.
